submitLabel: Your corpus test and refusal spec
intro: Paste the twenty-question test with each marked correct / wrong / stale but findable / absent, then the refusal spec, the named corpus owner and review cadence, and the make-good, followed by the 250–350 word write-up including your position on this module's claim. Resubmission is free and unlimited: the score is a mirror, not a gate.
activityContext:
You're grading a learner submission for AI 301 · The Specialist, Employee Experience / Internal Comms track. Module 8 applied activity: the workforce's twenty most common REAL questions (from tickets, search logs, or questions the team is actually asked, not invented), each tested against the organization's current knowledge base or intranet search and marked correct / wrong / stale but findable / absent; a refusal spec naming the categories the assistant must not answer, the escalation path INCLUDING what context travels with the employee, the named destination, and the register to use on disclosure categories; the named owner of corpus accuracy with a review cadence; and a make-good decided in advance for when the assistant is wrong and someone relies on it.

A learner with no assistant deployed should test against intranet search. That corpus is what an assistant would be built on, so the finding is the same. Don't treat 'we don't have one' as a reason the activity wasn't done.

A LOW correct count is a strong result, not a weak one. A learner who discovers their corpus answers six of twenty correctly and reports it plainly has produced the most valuable possible output of this module. Never grade the corpus quality; grade the honesty and specificity of the test.

The disclosure-category refusal is the module's central idea. A refusal spec that covers individual-case and medical questions but has nothing about questions that are disclosures (harassment, safety concerns, whistleblowing) has missed it, and feedback should say so directly.

The make-good is the other thing to check hard. 'We would apologize and look into it' is an improvisation, not a make-good. A named remedy decided in advance is what the module asks for, and a disclaimer offered in place of one should be named as decoration.

This track scores the delta rather than the score. Grade the learner's ACCOUNT of the gap between how many of the twenty they predicted their corpus could answer and how many it actually did — direction, size, and what it reveals. NEVER grade prediction accuracy.

opening.label: Predicted — of your workforce's top 20 questions, how many your knowledge base answers correctly today
opening.hint: Out of 20. Before you test it.

calibration.label: Tested — how many were actually correct
calibration.hint: Correct only. Stale-but-findable and absent don't count. A low number honestly arrived at is the best result this module produces.

dimensions.name: The twenty questions are real and sourced
dimensions.criteria: Drawn from tickets, search logs, or questions the team is genuinely asked (ideally from the Module 7 inventory) rather than imagined. Specific enough to be recognizably this organization's. Invented questions produce an invented test, and the whole activity rests on this step.

dimensions.name: The corpus test is honest and four-way
dimensions.criteria: Each question marked correct, wrong, stale but findable, or absent, against what the corpus actually returns rather than what the learner believes is in there. The stale-but-findable category is the one that reveals content debt and shouldn't be collapsed into 'correct'. A low correct count reported plainly is the strongest possible result and must be scored as such.

dimensions.name: The refusal spec includes the disclosure category
dimensions.criteria: Three kinds of refusal, and the third is the one that matters: individual-case questions, leave and medical questions, and questions that are disclosures wearing a question's clothes: harassment, safety, whistleblowing, resignation intent. A spec covering only the first two has missed the module's central idea. Also look for the discrimination the exercise teaches: not every sensitive-sounding question is a disclosure, and an over-broad list that refuses ordinary informational questions is its own failure.

dimensions.name: Escalation carries context to a named destination
dimensions.criteria: What information travels with the employee so they don't retype what they already wrote, a named person rather than a queue, and a stated register for disclosure categories. A refusal that dead-ends into 'please contact HR' should be named in feedback as leaving the employee worse off than if the assistant hadn't existed.

dimensions.name: Ownership, make-good, and the position
dimensions.criteria: A named owner of corpus accuracy (not the platform, the accuracy) with a review cadence, and a make-good decided in advance rather than improvised. 'We'd apologize and investigate' isn't a make-good; a named remedy is. Plus a committed position on the claim, engaging the strongest case against it: that the comparison isn't perfection but the status quo of a stale intranet and a three-day inbox, and that a strict refusal list mostly refuses the questions people most need answered. The strongest submissions state what the realistic alternative in their own organization actually is.
